TCU enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 22-10 overall and 11-7 in Big 12 play after beating Oklahoma State 95-88 in the Big 12 second round on March 11, 2026, then losing to Kansas 78-73 on March 12. ESPN’s schedule page lists the Frogs as 21-10, 11-7 after the regular season finale against Cincinnati on March 7, and 22-10 after the Oklahoma State win. TCU was selected to face Ohio State on Thursday, March 19, 2026. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/2628))

From a traditional scouting perspective, TCU’s identity starts with physicality, second-shot offense, and line-drive downhill guards rather than pretty half-court spacing. The raw profile backs that up: across 33 games, TCU averages 78.3 points, shoots 44.8 percent from the field, 33.1 percent from three, and owns a +3.0 rebound margin at 36.2 rebounds per game; opponents average 72.1 points. The assist total is notable too: 516 assists in 33 games, or 15.6 per game by calculation, with Brock Harding alone at 188 assists. This is not a pure isolation team. They play through paint touches, drive-and-kick action, and interior activity from Xavier Edmonds and David Punch, then rely on offensive rebounding and free throws to finish possessions. ([gofrogs.com](https://gofrogs.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Specific offensive tendencies show up in game evidence. Against Oklahoma State in the Big 12 Tournament on March 11, TCU scored 95 points with 19 offensive rebounds that turned into 27 second-chance points, and Tanner Toolson produced multiple put-back baskets off the bench. That is a clean example of the Frogs using shot attempts as entry passes to their frontcourt pressure on the glass. Against Arizona State on February 24, TCU shot only 32.4 percent in the first half, yet still led 33-30 because it attacked the foul line and the offensive interior; in the second half it shot 53.3 percent and used a 20-4 run once the game tilted into dribble penetration and paint collapse. Against Cincinnati on March 7, TCU posted 21 assists on 26 made field goals, which points to a ball-movement heavy game built on paint touches and kick-outs rather than stagnant one-on-one offense. ([gofrogs.com](https://gofrogs.com/news/2026/3/12/mens-basketball-punch-leads-frogs-past-cowboys-95-88))

Their half-court staples, based on shot-distribution evidence and personnel usage, are high ball screens for Jayden Pierre and Brock Harding, duck-ins/post seals for Edmonds, and slot or wing reversal into deep catch-and-shoot looks for Pierre and Liutauras Lelevicius. That is an inference from how points are created: Pierre has 51 made threes, Lelevicius 46, Micah Robinson 38, and Harding 188 assists; Edmonds shoots 57.2 percent from the field and has 219 rebounds, while Punch leads the team with 458 points and draws contact despite only 25.6 percent from three. In practice, that means TCU often runs through a guard entry, gets the defense rotating, and then either feeds Edmonds around the rim or drives the lane for fouls and cleanup chances. ([gofrogs.com](https://gofrogs.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Defensively, the philosophy is more rugged than schematic. TCU wants to turn the game into a rebounding and possession battle. The season numbers show 254 steals and 150 blocks in 33 games, while TCU Athletics notes the Frogs rank third in the Big 12 in steals per game and third in fastbreak points. They pressure the ball enough to create live-ball mistakes, but the more repeatable trait is finishing the stop with a rebound. TCU improved to 18-3 when outrebounding opponents after the March 11 Oklahoma State game; that record point is the single best shorthand for their defensive success. Against Cincinnati, they forced 19 turnovers, the most by a TCU opponent in Big 12 play. Against Texas Tech on March 3, they held the Red Raiders to 36.0 percent shooting in the second half after allowing 53.6 percent in the first half, a clear adjustment from a softer first-half perimeter containment to a more disruptive, body-up second half. ([gofrogs.com](https://gofrogs.com/news/2026/3/9/mens-basketball-preview-big-12-tournament?utm_source=openai))

Jamie Dixon’s coaching stamp is still obvious: win the glass, shorten your mistakes, and trust older guards late. His documented adjustment history this season is strong. On March 3 at No. 10 Texas Tech, TCU changed the game after halftime by tightening up defensively, cutting Tech to 36.0 percent shooting in the second half and closing with four makes in its last five shots in a 73-65 win. On February 24 versus Arizona State, Dixon managed around extreme foul trouble to three starters; Edmonds played only 17 minutes, Pierre fouled out, Punch had four fouls, yet TCU still authored a 20-4 second-half run and won by 12. On February 7 versus Kansas State, TCU erased an 18-point first-half deficit and a 10-point deficit with 5:26 left, then closed on a 7-0 run. Those games show a coach willing to alter lineups, survive with bench minutes, and lean into game flow instead of forcing one rigid rotation. ([gofrogs.com](https://gofrogs.com/news/2026/3/3/mens-basketball-tcu-tops-no-10-texas-tech-73-65))

Late-game execution has been good enough to matter in March. The best example is February 10 against No. 5 Iowa State: TCU won 62-55 and scored the final 12 points; ESPN’s recap notes Jayden Pierre’s three put TCU ahead with 48 seconds left. On February 7 against Kansas State, TCU was down 82-77 with 1:29 left and finished on a 7-0 run; Edmonds scored six of those points, and with TCU up 83-82, Punch forced a turnover on P.J. Haggerty with 6.7 seconds left. On March 11 against Oklahoma State, TCU trailed 82-81 with 5:19 left, took the lead on the next possession, and held it to the buzzer while Oklahoma State went without a field goal for the final 3:21. The warning sign is January 6 at Kansas: TCU led by 16 with 11:32 left in regulation and still lost 104-100 in overtime, hurt by going 2-of-6 at the foul line in the final 1:34 of regulation. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/game/_/gameId/401827675/iowa-state-tcu))

Key players start with David Punch, the primary tone-setter. He leads TCU in scoring at 14.3 points per game and adds 6.7 rebounds, 63 blocks, and 43 steals in 32 games. His recent form is excellent: career-high 26 points against Oklahoma State on March 11, 19 points in the overtime road win at Oklahoma State on February 14, and 20 points with nine rebounds and five blocks in the January 6 overtime loss at Kansas. Punch is the power driver and foul-drawer, but also their best weak-side shot blocker. ([gofrogs.com](https://gofrogs.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Xavier Edmonds is the matchup swing piece. He averages 12.6 points and 6.6 rebounds while shooting 57.2 percent, and by early March he had stacked 10 double-doubles in a 12-game span before recording an 11th on March 11. His standout moments are loud: career-high 26 points and 10 rebounds in the comeback win over Kansas State on February 7; 20 points and 12 rebounds at No. 10 Texas Tech on March 3; 14 points and 13 rebounds against West Virginia on February 21. Edmonds is also a better face-up and short-roll scorer than old-school scouting reports might assume, with 21 made threes. ([gofrogs.com](https://gofrogs.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Jayden Pierre and Brock Harding run the perimeter. Pierre averages 10.5 points and 90 assists, with a team-high 51 made threes. He had 18 points versus Cincinnati on March 7, 14 at Texas Tech on March 3, and the go-ahead three late versus Iowa State on February 10. Harding averages 8.0 points but has 188 assists, by far the team lead; his 11-assist double-double against Arizona State on February 24 is the cleanest example of him controlling game flow. Micah Robinson, at 10.5 points per game, has become an X-factor since entering the starting lineup; TCU was 7-1 after that move entering the Big 12 Tournament and 8-1 after the March 11 win. Robinson scored 20 against Arizona State and 15 at Texas Tech. Tanner Toolson is the bench microwave and effort rebounder: 17 points and 10 boards against Iowa State, plus 19 off the bench against Oklahoma State in Kansas City. ([gofrogs.com](https://gofrogs.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26))

Their notable wins reveal a dangerous tournament team. The February 10 win over No. 5 Iowa State, 62-55, showed they can win ugly against elite defense. The March 3 road win at No. 10 Texas Tech, 73-65, showed they can rebound and defend well enough away from home to beat a protected-seed caliber team. The February 7 comeback over Kansas State, 84-82, showed resilience after trailing by 18. The February 14 overtime road win at Oklahoma State, 95-92, showed poise in a high-possession late-game environment. Their notable losses are instructive too: January 6 at Kansas, 104-100 in OT, exposed late free-throw volatility; February 1 at Colorado, 87-61, was a major defensive breakdown; February 17 at UCF, 82-71, was a bubble-damaging road loss that underscored how average their offense can look when the glass edge disappears. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/game/_/gameId/401827675/iowa-state-tcu))

As for NCAA tournament history, Jamie Dixon is one of 11 active head coaches with at least 15 NCAA appearances, according to TCU’s March 9 release. His deepest documented run was the 2009 Elite Eight at Pittsburgh, and he also reached the Sweet 16 in 2004 and 2007. The record in the available sources does not show a deeper TCU run under Dixon than the Round of 32; the cited history specifically confirms Sweet 16 trips in 2004 and 2007 and Elite Eight in 2009 at Pitt. ([gofrogs.com](https://gofrogs.com/news/2026/3/9/mens-basketball-preview-big-12-tournament?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: TCU is not a beautiful team, but it is a hard team. The Frogs win with extra possessions, hard rebounding, rim pressure, and a frontcourt anchored by Punch and Edmonds. If Ohio State cannot keep Edmonds and Punch off the glass and cannot handle Pierre/Harding late in the clock, TCU has already shown in exact games this season that it can win rock fights, comeback games, and road NCAA-type games. ([gofrogs.com](https://gofrogs.com/news/2026/3/12/mens-basketball-punch-leads-frogs-past-cowboys-95-88))

TCU enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament profile as a classic high-variance, analytically mixed Big 12 team: good enough to beat elite opponents, flawed enough to leave the model ecosystem only cautiously optimistic. On the résumé side, the Horned Frogs were 22-10 against Division I competition and 11-7 in the Big 12, with a Warren Nolan team sheet showing a NET of 41, KPI 37, SOR 33, WAB 33, KenPom/POM 44, Bart Torvik T-Rank 48, and ESPN BPI 48. That same sheet lists a 6-6 record in Quadrant 1, 7-2 in Quadrant 2, and an overall NET strength of schedule of 51. A March 12 Bubble Watch snapshot from Frogs O’ War had them slightly lower a few days earlier — NET 47, KenPom 51, BPI 54, SOS 36 — which is useful context because it shows the profile improved late rather than being steadily dominant all season. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=TCU))

From a possession-based standpoint, the cleanest exact season numbers publicly accessible came from Sports-Reference’s advanced team page. TCU’s season adjusted-style box metrics there show a 69.5-possession tempo, an offensive rating of 110.8 points per 100 possessions, and a defensive rating of 101.4, for a net margin of +9.4 per 100. Their effective field-goal percentage was .545 on offense while allowing .509 defensively. They posted a 52.0% offensive rebounding rate proxy in the site’s rebound split framework, a 58.5% defensive rebounding figure, offensive turnovers of 11.3 per game versus 12.6 forced, and 13.3 threes made/attempt-context units alongside 34.1 twos, implying a roughly 28.1% three-point attempt share by simple shot mix calculation. Sports-Reference also lists TCU’s schedule strength at 9.30 and SRS at 15.88, while the team page gives 77.9 points scored and 71.4 allowed per game. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/seasons/men/2026-advanced-school-stats.html?utm_source=openai))

Those numbers point to the first major analytical conclusion: TCU is more defense-and-glass driven than public perception may assume, even if the offense has had explosive nights. The offense is not bad, but 110.8 ORtg is much closer to solid than elite. The defense, at 101.4 points allowed per 100 possessions, is the sturdier side of the profile, and that aligns with Jamie Dixon’s broader program identity. The team’s conventional stat line in Kansas State’s February game notes reinforces that shape: 78.7 points per game on 45.6% shooting and 33.4% from three, while allowing 71.5 points on 43.7% shooting and 34.2% from deep, with only 11.2 turnovers per game. Those same notes had TCU ranked 53rd in both NET and KenPom as of February 5, before the late push improved the résumé. ([kstatesports.com](https://www.kstatesports.com/documents/download/2026/2/5/23_Game_Notes_TCU.pdf))

If you are looking for the Four Factors lens, the most defensible exact values available are eFG% and the inferred shot-distribution data from Sports-Reference, plus game-level advanced splits from RealGM and Sports-Reference box scores. Season-wide, TCU’s .545 eFG% is comfortably positive, and the .509 opponent eFG% allowed suggests real resistance rather than just luck. The three-point attempt rate, however, is relatively modest at about 28.1%, which implies this is not a bomb-away offense. That matters: when TCU passes the eye test, it is often because the Frogs are physically disruptive, getting downhill, extending possessions, and winning the athletic exchanges — not because they are an elite spacing-and-volume-jump-shooting machine. Their publicly visible season percentages also support that interpretation: 45.6% from the field, 33.4% from three, and 72.0% at the line in the February notes. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/seasons/men/2026-advanced-school-stats.html?utm_source=openai))

Recent form is where the profile gets much more interesting. By early March, TCU had won seven of its last eight, including a road win at Texas Tech; ESPN’s recap of that March 3 result explicitly noted the Frogs were 20-10 overall and had won seven of eight during their push. Their Warren Nolan sheet later reflected the final effect of that surge: Q1 improved to 6-6, and the predictive metrics climbed into the 40s rather than the low-50s. In other words, the trajectory was positive even if the full-season body of work remained uneven. That late rise also explains the divergence between a middling season-long efficiency profile and a more dangerous tournament reputation. TCU was playing better than its full-year averages at the finish. ([espn.in](https://www.espn.in/mens-college-basketball/recap/_/gameId/401827719?utm_source=openai))

The best example of TCU’s volatility is in the game log itself. Sports-Reference shows losses to New Orleans and Michigan in November, but also a neutral-floor win over Florida and later top-end league wins over Iowa State and Texas Tech. Frogs O’ War summarized the résumé accurately as “confounding,” citing elite wins over Florida and Iowa State, near-misses against Michigan, BYU, and Kansas, plus damaging losses like New Orleans and Utah. That is exactly how the statistical profile reads: the median TCU performance is that of a good-but-not-great tournament team, while the 75th-percentile performance is strong enough to beat seeded opponents. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/texas-christian/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Where do the numbers diverge from conventional wisdom or the eye test? First, TCU may look more explosive than it really is because its best wins came in high-visibility settings against elite opponents. But the season offense is only moderately efficient, and the shot profile does not scream modern high-volume perimeter attack. Second, the team may look merely “scrappy” on defense, yet the underlying numbers suggest the defense is the more reliable tournament equity source. Third, the résumé’s jagged shape can make TCU seem fraudulent to skeptics, but a .500 Q1 record and top-50 standing across NET, KenPom, BPI, and T-Rank say this is not a fluke bubble team; it is a legitimately solid team with bad losses baked into the distribution. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=TCU))

Bottom line: TCU projects as a dangerous but imperfect 2026 tournament team. The exact public data I could verify paints them as roughly a top-40 to top-50 team nationally by the major predictive systems, with a NET in the low 40s, a BPI/POM/T-Rank cluster in the mid-to-high 40s, a pace just under 70 possessions per 40 minutes, offensive efficiency around 110.8, defensive efficiency around 101.4, and a strong-enough Q1/Q2 record to justify inclusion. The offense is functional rather than overwhelming; the defense and physicality are the true backbone; and the late-season trend indicates they were more dangerous in March than their full-season averages alone would suggest. That combination makes TCU the sort of team higher seeds do not want to see in the first weekend. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/team-net-sheet?team=TCU))
matchup-analyst:
TCU enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a team that wants to win with pressure, paint scoring, and foul pressure more than with pure perimeter shot-making. Through March 12, 2026, the Horned Frogs were 22-11, averaged 78.3 points, shot 44.8% from the field, only 33.1% from three, but got to the line often enough to make 16.6 free throws per game; they also forced 13.8 opponent turnovers per game while committing only 10.9 themselves. Their pace has been around 70.5 possessions per 40 minutes, which is moderately fast rather than extreme, and their offense is built less on elegant ball movement than on downhill guards feeding strong, physical forwards like David Punch and Xavier Edmonds. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/gofrogs.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

The core style is clear in the player usage and production. David Punch, a 6-foot-7, 246-pound forward, leads them with 14.3 points and 6.7 rebounds while also supplying 63 blocks; Xavier Edmonds, a 6-foot-8, 245-pound forward, adds 12.6 points and 6.6 rebounds on 57.2% shooting; Brock Harding, a 6-foot guard, is the primary organizer with 188 assists against 63 turnovers; Jayden Pierre, another 6-foot guard, adds 10.5 points and 90 assists; Micah Robinson gives them another physical 6-foot-6, 232-pound scorer off the wing/forward line. That tells you what TCU is: two small playmaking guards, then a heavy, muscular wing-forward front line that tries to overwhelm smaller teams around the elbows, slot drives, offensive glass, and late-clock bully finishes. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/gofrogs.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

The specific tactics that disrupt this style are the ones that deny straight-line drives and force them into jump-shot volume. TCU shot only 33.1% from three on the season and just 32.3% in conference play, so the math says opponents should load gaps, stunt hard at Punch and Edmonds, and make Pierre, Harding, Robinson, and Toolson beat them over a full game from the arc. Arizona provided a concrete example on January 10, 2026: TCU fell behind 43-27 at halftime, trailed by as many as 21, and never led in an 86-73 loss. Arizona’s size and shotmaking flipped the terms of the game, and TCU’s comeback run still depended heavily on Tanner Toolson’s bench scoring burst rather than sustained half-court creation. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/gofrogs.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Against pressure and ball disruption, there is evidence of vulnerability even though TCU’s raw turnover rate is decent overall. UCF’s 82-71 win on February 17 is the cleanest example: the Knights forced three TCU turnovers in a 1:39 stretch early, held TCU to nine assists, and held them to 19% from three while producing 17 assists themselves. That game matters because it shows that when opponents speed up TCU’s decision-making without giving up paint catches, the Frogs can become stagnant and overly individual. Their two small lead guards are skilled, but both are 6-foot-0, so length at the point of attack can shrink passing windows. ([ucfknights.com](https://ucfknights.com/news/2026/02/18/mens-hoops-snaps-three-game-slide-with-82-71-win-over-tcu))

On zone vulnerability, the season-long evidence points to a team that is attackable with compact help principles because it is not a high-level three-point group and is only average in assisted offense. TCU had 516 assists on 896 made field goals, an assist rate around 57.6%, and RealGM lists the team AST% at 59.4 with a pace of 70.5. That is not a pure isolation team, but it is also not a pass-happy spread offense that automatically shreds zones with skip-skip actions. The practical implication: a 2-3 or matchup zone that sinks hard on Punch/Edmonds and challenges Harding/Pierre to win with over-the-top shooting is viable, especially if the zone can rebound. Arizona and Colorado are useful game examples because both held TCU below 1.0 point per possession by keeping them from dictating interior terms; RealGM’s split page shows TCU with just a 90.9 offensive rating against Colorado and 96.8 against Arizona. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/gofrogs.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Preferred pace is another key lever. TCU is best when games live in the upper-60s to low-70s and become physical, possession-trading contests where its forwards can wear on you. In wins over Oklahoma State in the Big 12 tournament and at Baylor, TCU scored 95 and 97 respectively, but those games still reflected their preferred rhythm: repeated paint pressure, free throws, and strong interior finishing rather than a pure three-point avalanche. Against Baylor on January 24, TCU went on a 31-11 second-half run; against Oklahoma State on March 11, they erased a second-half deficit and got 26 from Punch plus a second-half shotmaking lift from Pierre. If you want to beat them, you must force the opposite: either drag them into a slower, more surgical half-court execution test where every possession requires multiple reversals, or make them play from behind against superior spacing so their physicality matters less. Colorado’s 87-61 win is the most alarming pace-control data point because TCU’s split offensive rating in that matchup was only 90.9. ([baylorbears.com](https://baylorbears.com/news/2026/1/24/mens-basketball-recap-vs-tcu?utm_source=openai))

Position-by-position mismatch analysis matters. At point guard, Harding and Pierre are both only 6-foot-0, so big guards can shoot over them or post them in switches; the counter is that Harding’s 188 assists and 56 steals make him disruptive if your guard is loose with the ball. At the 2/3, Lelevicius is 6-foot-7 and Toolson/Jace Posey are 6-foot-5, giving TCU some wing size, but only Lelevicius is a clearly efficient floor spacer at 39.7% from three. Robinson is physically strong at 6-foot-6, 232, yet shot only 38.6% overall and 31.7% from three, so disciplined closeouts can sit on his drive. The real strength is the 4/5 line: Punch at 6-foot-7, 246 and Edmonds at 6-foot-8, 245 can punish thinner frontcourts. The flip side is that truly long, mobile size can bother them; Arizona’s bigger frontline and Colorado’s interior resistance are examples where TCU did not impose itself. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/gofrogs.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Isolation versus team offense: TCU is not a pure isolation team, but it leans more toward direct creation than beautiful collective offense. The best percentage proxy available from current 2026 public team data is assist rate: TCU had assists on about 57.6% of made field goals overall (516 assists on 896 makes), while RealGM lists team AST% at 59.4. That suggests roughly 40%+ of their makes are unassisted or created in ways that finish without a direct assist, which fits the eye test of Pierre/Harding ball screens and Punch/Edmonds individual finishing. By comparison, in the UCF loss TCU had only nine assists, a sign that when you break their first action, they can fall into one-on-one or late-clock bailout basketball. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/gofrogs.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Transition profile: the best available public 2026 team-level pace data shows TCU at 70.5 possessions per 40, so they are neither a plodding team nor a full-throttle transition team every trip. Their transition offense is functionally driven by steals and live-ball pressure: 7.7 steals per game, +2.9 turnover margin, and 13.8 opponent turnovers forced per game. That means transition opportunities often come from defense first, not just run-after-make tempo. The defensive vulnerability is the inverse: when opponents protect the ball and make TCU guard second-side actions, the Frogs lose one of their easiest scoring sources. UCF’s 17 assists against only six turnovers before facing TCU, and 17 assists versus TCU in the win, is exactly the blueprint: deny live-ball runouts and make them score in the half court. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/gofrogs.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))

Coaching adaptability is a relative strength. Jamie Dixon’s team produced multiple in-game reversals this season. TCU erased an 18-point deficit to beat Kansas State 84-82 on February 7 behind Edmonds’ 26 points. They also used a 31-11 second-half run to win 97-90 at Baylor on January 24, and rallied from a double-digit second-half deficit to beat Oklahoma State 95-88 in the Big 12 tournament on March 11. Those are not hypothetical “culture” arguments; they are named comeback games, which indicate a staff willing to change coverage, rotate scoring burden, and trust different closers from game to game. ([gofrogs.com](https://gofrogs.com/news/2026/2/7/mens-basketball-edmonds-leads-tcu-to-comeback-win-over-k-state-84-82))

Concrete game plan: To beat TCU you must wall off Punch and Edmonds early, force Pierre/Harding into length, and win the possession game without feeding their transition offense. Go under selectively against Harding until he proves the jumper, crowd Pierre’s driving hand, and top-lock Lelevicius as the one wing spacer who can really punish clean catch-and-shoot looks at 39.7% from three. On the other end, attack the 6-foot-0 guards with size in ball screens and post-switches, make Punch defend in space, and force Edmonds to guard multiple actions instead of just finishing plays. Most importantly, do not let TCU generate easy points from steals; their identity strengthens when the game becomes chaotic. The evidence says the best blueprint is the UCF/Arizona/Colorado model: value the ball, load gaps, make TCU a jump-shooting team, and keep them from winning with physical paint touches and second-half momentum runs. ([s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com](https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/sidearm.nextgen.sites/gofrogs.com/stats/mbball/2025/pdf/cume.pdf))
